name: Certified Implementation Specialist – IT Service Management
note: ServiceNow uses an unpublished cut score for CIS-ITSM; community consensus puts it near 70%. Treat 85% here as your readiness bar. Domain weights follow the January 2026 blueprint. Items marked release-sensitive reference state names, workspaces, and features that change between releases; verify them against your own instance.

questions.stem: Which framework are ServiceNow's ITSM processes primarily aligned with?
options: COBIT 5 for audit planning
PMBOK project phases
ITIL
Six Sigma DMAIC cycles
questions.explanation: ServiceNow's ITSM applications follow ITIL practices for incident, problem, change, and request management. The other frameworks address governance, projects, and quality.

questions.stem: How do incident, problem, and change management typically relate?
options: Incidents reveal problems, and problems are fixed through changes
Problems are closed first, and incidents are opened to confirm them
They're independent processes that never reference each other
Changes create problems, which are then turned into new incidents
questions.explanation: Incidents restore service, problem management finds root causes behind them, and changes implement permanent fixes. The records link to each other on the platform.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an incident and a service request?
options: An incident is always minor; a request is always urgent and critical
There's no difference; both are logged on the same table and form
An incident is an unplanned disruption; a request asks for something
A request is raised only by IT staff; an incident only by end users
questions.explanation: Incidents restore normal service. Requests ask for standard things like access or equipment. Either can come from anyone, and they use different tables and processes.

questions.stem: Which certification is a prerequisite before registering for CIS-ITSM?
options: CIS-Event Management
CIS-Discovery only
Certified Application Developer
CIS-Data Foundations
questions.explanation: CIS-ITSM requires CSA and CIS-Data Foundations, reflecting how much ITSM depends on good CMDB data. Discovery, Event Management, and CAD aren't prerequisites.

questions.stem: Which role is typically given to service desk agents working incidents, problems, and changes?
options: snc_external, for portal access
security_admin, for elevated tasks
admin, for full access
itil
questions.explanation: The itil role grants fulfiller access to core ITSM processes. Admin and security_admin are excessive, and snc_external is for external portal users.

questions.stem: Where do agents typically work ITSM records in recent releases?
options: Service Operations Workspace
The CMDB CI Class Manager
The system log list for each table
The Service Portal page designer
questions.explanation: Service Operations Workspace gives agents a modern, unified experience for incidents, problems, changes, and requests. Logs, Class Manager, and the portal designer aren't agent workspaces.

questions.stem: Why does ITSM depend on good CMDB data?
options: It stores the incident numbers for each ticket
It drives impact, routing, and change risk
It approves every normal change automatically
It replaces the need for assignment groups
questions.explanation: Knowing which CI and service are affected informs priority, assignment, and change risk and conflict detection. The CMDB doesn't number tickets, replace groups, or approve changes.

questions.stem: Why do incident and change forms include Service and Service offering fields under CSDM?
options: To record which business service and offering is affected
To decide which instance the record is stored on
To store the agent's preferred service desk language
To set the record's color in list views
questions.explanation: CSDM-aligned service fields link work to what the business consumes, improving impact assessment and reporting. Language, storage, and colors aren't involved.

questions.stem: What does "task" mean as a table in ITSM?
options: A personal to-do list that each agent keeps for reminders
A report showing the number of tasks closed today
A table used only for HR onboarding activities
The base table that incident, problem, and change extend
questions.explanation: Task is the parent table providing shared fields and behavior. It isn't a personal list, HR-only, or a report.

questions.stem: What is a good starting point for an ITSM implementation?
options: Implement all ITSM modules at once without priorities
Build custom tables to replace incident and change
Customize every form before gathering any requirements
Adopt base processes, then tailor where justified
questions.explanation: Starting from base functionality speeds value and keeps upgrades simple. Heavy customization, replacing core tables, or big-bang rollouts add risk.

questions.stem: What's the purpose of linking related ITSM records, such as an incident to its problem?
options: To keep the full story traceable across processes
To prevent either record from ever being closed
To copy the assignment group between records
To merge the records into one when either closes
questions.explanation: Links show how disruptions, root causes, and fixes connect. They don't merge records, block closure, or copy assignments.

questions.stem: What does Now Assist add to ITSM for agents?
options: Automatic approval of every pending change request
A replacement for assignment groups and their members
A second database that stores every incident twice
Generative AI help, like summaries and resolution notes
questions.explanation: Now Assist provides AI skills such as summarizing records and drafting resolution notes, depending on licensing and configuration. It doesn't duplicate data, approve changes, or replace groups.

questions.stem: What does Predictive Intelligence help with in ITSM?
options: Writing code fixes for application defects automatically
Predicting the date of the next ServiceNow release
Suggesting category, assignment, or similar records
Encrypting sensitive fields on incident records
questions.explanation: Machine learning models classify and route records and find similar ones. They don't write code, predict releases, or encrypt data.

questions.stem: Why separate fulfiller and end-user experiences in ITSM?
options: End users aren't allowed to see their own tickets
Fulfillers can only use the classic interface
The platform requires two separate instances
Each needs different tools and information
questions.explanation: Agents need workspaces and full records, while end users need simple portals to request help and track status. Users can see their own tickets, fulfillers can use workspaces, and it's one instance.

questions.stem: What's the value of a knowledge base in ITSM?
options: It stores the instance's update sets
It replaces the incident table entirely
It speeds resolution and enables self-service
It sets SLA targets for each team
questions.explanation: Knowledge helps agents resolve issues and lets users help themselves, reducing incident volume. It doesn't replace incidents, store update sets, or set SLAs.

questions.stem: How is incident priority usually calculated?
options: From impact and urgency
From the caller's job title only
From the time of day the incident is opened
From the number of characters in the description
questions.explanation: A priority lookup combines impact and urgency. Job titles, description length, and time of day don't set priority in the base process.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the "On Hold" state for an incident?
options: Hiding the incident from the caller's portal view
Escalating the incident to the highest priority level
Pausing work while waiting on something, like the caller
Closing the incident permanently without a resolution
questions.explanation: On Hold, with reasons such as awaiting caller, change, problem, or vendor, shows the agent is blocked and can pause SLAs. It doesn't close, escalate, or hide the incident.

questions.stem: What typically happens when the caller adds a comment to a resolved incident?
options: It's sent to the CAB
It becomes a problem record
It can reopen to In Progress
It's deleted from the system
questions.explanation: Caller responses on resolved incidents often reopen them, since the issue may not be fixed. Deletion, conversion to problems, or CAB review aren't triggered.

questions.stem: What happens to resolved incidents if the caller doesn't respond?
options: They're automatically reopened each week
They're deleted at the end of the month
They stay resolved forever with no change
They auto-close after a configured period
questions.explanation: An auto-close setting moves resolved incidents to Closed after a set time. They don't stay resolved indefinitely, get deleted, or reopen on a schedule.

questions.stem: An outage generates 200 incidents for the same email problem. How should they be managed?
options: Close all of them and ask users to call later
Work each of the 200 incidents separately
Link them as children of one parent incident
Convert all 200 into separate problem records
questions.explanation: Parent-child relationships let agents manage one parent, with child incidents updated and resolved alongside it. Working them separately wastes effort, and closing or converting them all is wrong.

questions.stem: What does Major Incident Management add?
options: An automatic priority of 5 for all incidents
A way to delete incidents with low priority
A replacement for the change advisory board
A structured process for high-impact incidents
questions.explanation: MIM adds proposal and acceptance of major incidents, a dedicated workbench, communication plans, and post-incident review. It doesn't delete, reprioritize everything, or replace CAB.

questions.stem: Who typically accepts a proposed major incident?
options: A major incident manager
Any member of the service desk
The external vendor involved
The caller who reported it
questions.explanation: Agents propose major incidents, and major incident managers decide whether to accept them. Callers, all agents, or vendors don't make that call.

questions.stem: Why use communication plans during a major incident?
options: To assign the incident to a new support group
To allow callers to approve the final resolution
To send regular, targeted updates to stakeholders
To schedule the incident's post-mortem meeting
questions.explanation: Communication plans define who gets updates, how, and how often, keeping stakeholders informed. Approvals, scheduling, and reassignment are separate.

questions.stem: An agent resolves an incident with a known fix. What helps the next agent resolve it faster?
options: Copying the notes into a personal email
Attaching or creating a knowledge article
Changing the category to "Other"
Closing the incident without any notes
questions.explanation: Knowledge captures fixes for reuse. Personal email, empty notes, or vague categories don't help anyone else.

questions.stem: What is an incident task used for?
options: Recording the caller's satisfaction score
Requesting approval for the incident's priority
Scheduling a change to fix the root cause
Assigning part of the work to another group
questions.explanation: Incident tasks split work — such as on-site support — while the parent incident stays with the main team. Surveys, priority approvals, and changes are separate.

questions.stem: Which field shows who reported the incident, as opposed to who logged it?
options: Resolved by
Assigned to
Opened by
Caller
questions.explanation: The caller is the affected person reporting the issue. Opened by records who created the record, assigned to is the agent, and resolved by is who fixed it.

questions.stem: An incident needs to be routed automatically to the network team when its category is Network. What should be configured?
options: A business rule that emails the team lead
A knowledge base article about networks
An assignment rule or data lookup
A UI policy that hides the group field
questions.explanation: Assignment rules and data lookups set assignment groups from conditions. Emailing a lead, hiding fields, or writing articles doesn't route the record.

questions.stem: What's the difference between impact and urgency?
options: They're two names for the same field on the incident form
Urgency is how many users are affected; impact is how fast to fix
Impact is how widespread; urgency is how quickly it must be fixed
Impact is set by the agent; urgency is always set by the system
questions.explanation: Impact measures the scope of the effect, and urgency measures time sensitivity. Together they determine priority.

questions.stem: What happens to child incidents when the parent incident is resolved?
options: They become problem records
They're reassigned to the caller
They're typically resolved with it
They're deleted from the system
questions.explanation: Child incidents follow the parent's resolution by default, so users get updates without separate work. They aren't deleted, converted, or reassigned to callers.

questions.stem: An incident is caused by a known problem with no permanent fix yet. What should the agent use?
options: The known error's workaround
A deletion of the incident record
A new change request for every user
A request to the CAB for approval
questions.explanation: Workarounds from known errors restore service quickly while problem management works on the permanent fix. New changes per user, deletion, or CAB review aren't appropriate.

questions.stem: What's the main goal of incident management?
options: Restoring service quickly
Approving changes to production systems
Finding the root cause of every incident
Fulfilling requests for new equipment
questions.explanation: Incident management focuses on restoring service. Root cause belongs to problem management, change approval to change management, and equipment to request management.

questions.stem: How can an end user check the status of their incident?
options: By reading the system log
Through the self-service portal
By asking for the admin role
By opening the CMDB
questions.explanation: Portals let users see their tickets and add comments. Logs, admin roles, and the CMDB aren't for end users.

questions.stem: What is an "interaction" record used for?
options: Recording changes approved during a CAB meeting
Storing the root cause analysis for a problem
Logging contacts, like chats, before triage
Tracking SLA pauses on a requested item
questions.explanation: Interactions capture inbound contacts — chat, phone, walk-up — and can lead to incidents, requests, or resolution without a ticket. The other options belong to other records.

questions.stem: Why should agents choose the affected configuration item on an incident?
options: To retire the CI from the CMDB
To stop the CI from being discovered
To assign the CI's owner as the caller
To show impact and link records
questions.explanation: The affected CI links the incident to services, changes, and problems, supporting impact analysis and trends. It doesn't change the caller, discovery, or lifecycle.

questions.stem: What does the "Resolved" state indicate compared with "Closed"?
options: The incident has been permanently archived
The incident is fixed, pending confirmation
The incident was canceled as a duplicate
The incident is waiting for the caller's reply
questions.explanation: Resolved means service is restored and the caller can confirm; Closed is final. Duplicates are canceled, and waiting on callers uses On Hold.

questions.stem: When should an incident be canceled rather than resolved?
options: When a related change was rejected by the CAB
When it was logged in error or is a duplicate
When the caller disagreed with the resolution
When the fix took longer than the SLA allowed
questions.explanation: Canceled is for records that shouldn't exist, such as duplicates. SLA breaches, disagreements, and rejected changes don't justify cancellation.

questions.stem: What's a sign that an incident should become a problem record?
options: The incident has more than three work notes
The incident was resolved within its SLA target
The caller is a senior executive in the company
The same issue keeps recurring with no root cause
questions.explanation: Recurring incidents without a known cause point to an underlying problem. Meeting SLAs, caller seniority, and note counts don't.

questions.stem: What does incident escalation typically mean?
options: Closing it so that a new incident can be opened
Moving it to more expertise or management
Hiding it from the caller until it's fixed
Lowering its priority to free up the service desk
questions.explanation: Functional escalation brings in more expertise; hierarchical escalation brings in management. Lowering priority, closing, or hiding aren't escalation.

questions.stem: Why use categories and subcategories on incidents?
options: To support routing, reporting, and trend spotting
To decide which instance stores the incident
To set the incident's number prefix
To encrypt the incident's description
questions.explanation: Good categorization drives assignment and analysis. It doesn't control storage, numbering, or encryption.

questions.stem: What should happen at the end of a major incident?
options: Immediate closure of all related changes
Removal of the incident from reports
Deletion of the major incident record
A post-incident review to capture lessons
questions.explanation: Post-incident reviews identify improvements and often lead to problem records. Deleting records, closing changes, or hiding data loses that value.

questions.stem: An agent can't fix an incident and needs specialist help. What should they do?
options: Leave it assigned to themselves indefinitely
Reassign it to the right group with clear notes
Close it and ask the caller to open a new one
Lower its priority so it stops breaching
questions.explanation: Clear reassignment with context gets the right expertise quickly. Closing, sitting on it, or gaming priority hurts the user and the metrics.

questions.stem: Which is a common way users report incidents besides calling the service desk?
options: Editing the CMDB directly as a user
Writing in the system properties table
The self-service portal or Virtual Agent
Sending a change request to the CAB
questions.explanation: Portals, Virtual Agent, and email are common self-service channels. Users don't edit the CMDB, properties, or raise changes to report issues.

questions.stem: What's the purpose of the resolution code and notes on an incident?
options: Deciding which group receives the next incident
Setting the incident's priority for future incidents
Approving the related change request
Recording how it was fixed for reporting and reuse
questions.explanation: Resolution details support knowledge, trend analysis, and audits. They don't set priority, routing, or approvals.

questions.stem: What does "first contact resolution" measure?
options: Incidents raised by first-time users of the portal
Incidents resolved without escalation or follow-up
Incidents that were opened on the first day of the month
Incidents assigned to the first group in the list
questions.explanation: FCR shows how often the service desk resolves issues immediately, a key efficiency and satisfaction indicator.

questions.stem: Why is the "Awaiting change" On Hold reason useful?
options: It cancels the incident until the change closes
It shows the fix depends on a scheduled change
It assigns the incident to the change manager
It approves the change request automatically
questions.explanation: The reason documents why the incident is blocked and can pause SLAs while a change is implemented. It doesn't approve, cancel, or reassign anything.

questions.stem: What is the main goal of problem management?
options: Finding and fixing the root causes of incidents
Fulfilling standard requests from the service catalog
Restoring service as quickly as possible for users
Approving changes before they go into production
questions.explanation: Problem management prevents incidents by addressing underlying causes. Restoring service is incident management, approvals are change management, and requests are request management.

questions.stem: What is a known error?
options: An incident that was logged by mistake and canceled
A problem with a known cause and documented workaround
A request that was rejected by the approver
A change that failed and had to be rolled back
questions.explanation: Known errors document a diagnosed problem and its workaround, helping agents resolve related incidents. Canceled incidents, failed changes, and rejected requests are different records.

questions.stem: How are known error workarounds commonly shared with agents?
options: Through the change schedule calendar
In the CMDB Health dashboard
As known error knowledge articles
Through the system properties list
questions.explanation: Publishing known errors to knowledge makes workarounds searchable when agents handle incidents. The change schedule, CMDB health, and properties don't share workarounds.

questions.stem: What's the difference between reactive and proactive problem management?
options: Reactive responds to incidents; proactive finds issues first
Reactive is done by users; proactive is done by vendors
Proactive only handles security; reactive handles everything else
There's no difference; both terms mean the same activity
questions.explanation: Reactive problem management investigates incidents that occurred, while proactive analysis uses trends and monitoring to prevent them. Neither is defined by who does it or by security scope.

questions.stem: In the current problem process, which state follows Resolved?
options: Fix in Progress
Assess
Closed
Root Cause Analysis
questions.explanation: A typical flow is New, Assess, Root Cause Analysis, Fix in Progress, Resolved, Closed.

questions.stem: What are problem tasks used for?
options: Recording each incident that's linked to the problem
Scheduling the CAB meeting for the problem
Assigning investigation or fix work to other teams
Approving the problem's priority before analysis
questions.explanation: Problem tasks — including root cause analysis tasks — distribute work while the problem tracks the overall effort. Linked incidents, priority approval, and CAB scheduling are separate.

questions.stem: A permanent fix for a problem requires a production change. What should happen?
options: Ask the caller to approve the fix
Apply the fix directly without any change
Raise a change request from the problem
Close the problem and open a new incident
questions.explanation: Fixes go through change management, linked to the problem for traceability. Bypassing change control, closing early, or asking callers to approve are wrong.

questions.stem: How does linking incidents to a problem help?
options: It deletes the incidents once the problem record is created
It prevents any further incidents on the same service
It changes every linked incident's priority to critical
It shows the problem's impact and updates incidents when fixed
questions.explanation: Links show scope and allow communicating workarounds and fixes to related incidents. Incidents aren't deleted, reprioritized, or prevented by linking.

questions.stem: What does root cause analysis aim to identify?
options: Which agent closed the most incidents
How many users reported the issue
Why it happened, not just what
Who should be blamed for the outage
questions.explanation: RCA finds the underlying cause so it can be fixed. Blame, counts, and agent stats aren't its goal.

questions.stem: Which technique asks "why" repeatedly to reach a root cause?
options: A SWOT analysis
A RACI chart
The 5 Whys
A Gantt chart
questions.explanation: The 5 Whys drills down through causes. RACI assigns roles, Gantt charts schedule work, and SWOT assesses strategy.

questions.stem: When should a problem be resolved?
options: When the root cause is fixed or the risk is accepted
When the first related incident is resolved
As soon as a workaround is documented and shared
Whenever the problem has been open for 30 days
questions.explanation: A workaround makes a problem a known error but doesn't resolve it. Resolution comes with a permanent fix or a decision to accept the risk.

questions.stem: Who is typically accountable for driving a problem to resolution?
options: The problem owner
The external auditor reviewing ITSM
The service desk agent on the next shift
The caller of the first related incident
questions.explanation: Problem owners coordinate investigation and fixes. Callers, random agents, and auditors don't drive problems.

questions.stem: What does trend analysis of incidents help problem managers do?
options: Assign incidents to the right agent faster
Spot recurring issues worth investigating
Calculate each agent's performance bonus
Approve emergency changes during an outage
questions.explanation: Trend analysis finds patterns that suggest underlying problems — the core of proactive problem management. It isn't for routing, compensation, or approvals.

questions.stem: Why mark a problem record as a known error even before it's fixed?
options: So agents can apply the workaround to new incidents
So the problem is removed from all open reports
So the related change is approved automatically
So the problem skips root cause analysis entirely
questions.explanation: Flagging a known error makes the workaround visible and reusable. It doesn't hide the problem, approve changes, or skip analysis.

questions.stem: Should every incident create a problem record?
options: Yes; but only for incidents opened by phone
No; problems are only created by vendors
No; usually only recurring or significant ones
Yes; every incident needs its own problem
questions.explanation: Problem management focuses effort where it prevents significant or repeated impact. One problem per incident would overwhelm teams.

questions.stem: What's the relationship between a problem's priority and its linked incidents?
options: Problem priority is chosen randomly by the system
Linked incidents don't affect problem priority
Impact across linked incidents can raise priority
The problem always copies the lowest incident priority
questions.explanation: Many or severe linked incidents increase a problem's business impact and therefore its priority. Priority isn't random or copied from the lowest incident.

questions.stem: A problem's root cause is in a vendor's product, and the vendor will fix it next quarter. What should the problem show?
options: A resolved state, since the vendor is responsible
Its status, the workaround, and the vendor dependency
A canceled state, because it can't be fixed internally
Nothing, since vendor issues aren't problems
questions.explanation: Documenting the dependency and workaround keeps the problem visible until the fix arrives. Resolving or canceling it early hides an open risk.

questions.stem: Why include a post-implementation check after a problem fix is deployed?
options: To reassign linked incidents
To delete the problem's knowledge article
To lower the problem's priority
To confirm incidents stopped
questions.explanation: Confirming that incidents stopped shows the root cause was really addressed. Deleting knowledge, lowering priority, or reassigning doesn't verify anything.

questions.stem: Which role typically has the authority to accept the risk of not fixing a problem?
options: The CMDB administrator for the affected CI
An appropriate manager or problem owner per policy
Any end user who was affected by the incidents
The service desk agent who logged the problem
questions.explanation: Risk acceptance needs someone accountable. End users, logging agents, and CMDB admins don't own that decision.

questions.stem: What does a "fishbone" (Ishikawa) diagram help with?
options: Mapping CI relationships in the CMDB
Organizing possible causes into categories
Calculating SLA breach percentages
Scheduling changes around blackout windows
questions.explanation: Fishbone diagrams structure brainstorming of causes, such as people, process, and technology. They aren't for scheduling, SLAs, or CMDB maps.

questions.stem: What's the benefit of reporting on known errors over time?
options: It shows which agents opened the most incidents
It shows how many users logged into the portal
It shows where workarounds replace fixes
It shows the number of changes approved by CAB
questions.explanation: A growing pile of known errors with only workarounds signals technical debt. The other reports measure different things.

questions.stem: What does a problem's "Fix in Progress" state indicate?
options: The problem has been canceled
The root cause is still unknown
A permanent fix is being implemented
The workaround has stopped working
questions.explanation: Fix in Progress means the cause is known and a fix is underway, often through a change. Unknown causes are still in analysis.

questions.stem: How can problem management reduce service desk workload?
options: By removing causes so fewer incidents happen
By closing incidents faster without fixes
By blocking users from opening new incidents
By reassigning incidents to other teams
questions.explanation: Fixing root causes prevents repeat incidents. Premature closure, blocking users, or shuffling work doesn't reduce real demand.

questions.stem: What are the three main change types in ServiceNow?
options: Internal, external, and vendor
Planned, unplanned, and urgent
Minor, major, and critical
Normal, standard, and emergency
questions.explanation: Normal changes follow full assessment and authorization, standard changes are pre-approved, and emergency changes are expedited.

questions.stem: What makes a standard change different from a normal change?
options: It doesn't need to be recorded at all
It can only be raised during an outage
It's pre-approved and low-risk, from a template
It needs CAB approval every single time it's used
questions.explanation: Standard changes are repeatable, low-risk, and pre-authorized, raised from the standard change catalog. Normal changes need assessment and authorization, and emergency changes handle urgent fixes. All changes are recorded.

questions.stem: How does a new change become a standard change template?
options: Through an approved standard change proposal
By any agent copying a normal change's fields
By the system after a change runs three times
By the CAB voting on it after each use
questions.explanation: Standard change proposals are reviewed and approved before templates join the catalog. Copying fields, repeated votes, or automatic promotion aren't the mechanism.

questions.stem: Which state sequence matches a normal change?
options: New, Closed, Review, Implement, Assess, Authorize
New, Assess, Authorize, Scheduled, Implement, Review, Closed
Draft, Approved, Implement, Closed, with no assessment
New, Implement, Authorize, Review, Assess, Scheduled, Closed
questions.explanation: Normal changes are assessed, authorized, scheduled, implemented, reviewed, and closed.

questions.stem: How does an emergency change differ in its lifecycle?
options: It can only be implemented during a blackout window
It skips Assess and is authorized quickly, often by an ECAB
It requires two full CAB meetings before it can proceed
It skips implementation and goes straight to Review
questions.explanation: Emergency changes are expedited, often authorized by an emergency CAB, then reviewed afterward. They still get implemented, don't need extra meetings, and shouldn't target blackout windows.

questions.stem: What does the CAB Workbench help change managers do?
options: Write the code that each change will deploy
Discover CIs that changes will affect
Plan CAB meetings and agendas
Resolve incidents caused by changes
questions.explanation: The CAB Workbench schedules meetings, builds agendas, and records decisions. Coding, discovery, and incident resolution happen elsewhere.

questions.stem: What does change conflict detection check for?
options: Overlaps with other changes or blackout windows on the same CIs
Whether the change's priority matches the incident's priority
Whether the requester has completed change training
Whether the change's description contains spelling mistakes
questions.explanation: Conflict detection checks schedules for the affected CIs — other changes, blackout periods, and maintenance windows. Spelling, training, and priority matching aren't conflicts.

questions.stem: What is a blackout window?
options: A period when changes aren't allowed
A period when the CAB doesn't meet
A period when incidents can't be opened
A period when changes must be implemented
questions.explanation: Blackout windows, such as financial close, block changes to reduce risk. Maintenance windows are when changes are preferred.

questions.stem: How is a change's risk typically determined?
options: From risk conditions and an assessment
From the length of the implementation plan
From the number of approvers assigned to it
From the requester's job title
questions.explanation: Risk comes from configured conditions (such as affected CI criticality) and assessment answers, and newer releases add data-driven risk scoring. Approver counts, plan length, and titles don't set risk.

questions.stem: What do change approval policies determine?
options: When the change will be implemented in production
Who must approve a change, based on its attributes
Which incident caused the change to be raised
Which CIs the change is allowed to affect
questions.explanation: Approval policies decide required approvals — for example, CAB for high risk, manager only for low risk. Scheduling, scope, and origin are other fields.

questions.stem: Why should every change include an implementation, backout, and test plan?
options: Because the CAB can't meet without three plans
So it can be done safely and reversed if it fails
So the requester can skip the risk assessment
So the change can be implemented in a blackout
questions.explanation: Plans make implementation repeatable and rollback possible. They don't replace risk assessment or permit work in blackout windows.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the Review state after implementation?
options: Confirming success and recording lessons
Scheduling the change into a maintenance window
Requesting approval from the change requester
Assessing the change's risk before authorization
questions.explanation: Post-implementation review checks outcomes and captures improvements. Risk, scheduling, and approvals happen earlier.

questions.stem: A change was implemented without approval. What is it called?
options: A standard change
A normal change
An emergency change
An unauthorized change
questions.explanation: Unauthorized changes bypass change control and often cause incidents. Standard changes are pre-approved, and emergency and normal changes are authorized.

questions.stem: Where can teams see all scheduled changes on a calendar?
options: The change schedule
The CMDB Health dashboard
The knowledge base
The problem workspace
questions.explanation: The change schedule shows planned changes, blackout periods, and maintenance windows. The other views don't show change timing.

questions.stem: What is a change model in recent releases?
options: A report of the most common reasons changes fail
A template for writing change descriptions
A diagram of how a CI connects to its services
A change type's states and transitions
questions.explanation: Change models define lifecycles and allowed transitions, letting organizations tailor change types. CI diagrams, failure reports, and description templates are different.

questions.stem: Why do change requests list affected CIs?
options: To assign the CI's owner as the change requester
To retire the CIs after implementation
To stop the CIs from being discovered
To support impact analysis, conflicts, and risk
questions.explanation: Affected CIs drive impacted services, conflicts, and risk. They don't change requesters, discovery, or lifecycle.

questions.stem: What does "change success rate" measure?
options: The number of standard change templates available
The time taken to approve a change request
The number of changes the CAB reviewed this month
The share of changes done without problems
questions.explanation: Success rate tracks how often changes go well, a key measure of change quality. Review counts, approval time, and template counts are other metrics.

questions.stem: What's an advantage of moving low-risk, repeatable changes to standard changes?
options: They skip testing in all cases
They speed delivery and reduce CAB workload
They automatically fix related problems
They no longer need to be recorded
questions.explanation: Pre-approval speeds routine work and frees CAB for risky changes. Standard changes are still recorded and should be tested.

questions.stem: What happens if a change is rejected during authorization?
options: It's automatically converted into an emergency change
It can't proceed and may be revised and resubmitted
It's implemented anyway because it was scheduled
It's deleted along with all its approval history
questions.explanation: Rejection stops the change. The requester can address feedback and resubmit. Implementing anyway, converting, or deleting would bypass control.

questions.stem: Who typically attends a CAB meeting?
options: Only the person who raised the change
Change managers and affected teams
Only external auditors
Every employee in the organization
questions.explanation: CABs bring together people who can assess risk and impact. Everyone, only the requester, or only auditors wouldn't serve that purpose.

questions.stem: What is an ECAB?
options: An email sent to CAB members after meetings
An external company that audits changes
A small group for emergency changes
An extended calendar of approved blackouts
questions.explanation: The emergency CAB is a smaller, faster group for urgent decisions. The other options aren't ECABs.

questions.stem: How can a change be linked to the incident it's meant to fix?
options: Through related records on the incident and change
By copying the incident's description into the change
By giving both records the same number
By assigning both to the same agent
questions.explanation: Related lists and reference fields connect incidents, problems, and changes. Copying text, sharing numbers, or same assignee don't create links.

questions.stem: What's the purpose of a maintenance window on a CI?
options: Showing preferred times for changes to that CI
Blocking any changes to that CI permanently
Hiding that CI from the CMDB
Pausing SLAs for incidents on that CI
questions.explanation: Maintenance windows indicate when changes are least disruptive, and conflict detection can flag changes outside them.

questions.stem: What does change risk assessment typically ask about?
options: Its impact, complexity, testing, and backout
The number of CIs in the CMDB
The requester's preferred working hours
The color of the change form
questions.explanation: Assessments gather information that drives risk. Working hours, form colors, and CMDB size are irrelevant.

questions.stem: An organization wants data-driven risk for changes based on past outcomes. What feature helps?
options: A rule that all changes are high risk
A larger CAB with more voting members
A knowledge article listing risky teams
Change success scores or risk intelligence
questions.explanation: Newer change features use history — team success rates, CI incident history — to calculate risk and enable automated approvals. A larger CAB, blanket high risk, or articles don't provide data-driven scoring.

questions.stem: Why connect DevOps pipelines to change management?
options: To let developers skip recording any production changes
To schedule CAB meetings inside the build tool
To replace the CMDB with the pipeline's own inventory
To create and approve changes from pipeline data
questions.explanation: DevOps change velocity lets pipelines create changes and use policy-based approval, keeping control while speeding delivery. It doesn't skip records, replace the CMDB, or move CAB.

questions.stem: What should happen if a change fails during implementation?
options: Close the change as successful to protect metrics
Leave the system as is and fix it next quarter
Delete the change and start over without notes
Follow the backout plan and record the outcome
questions.explanation: The backout plan restores service, and recording the failure supports review and learning. Hiding or ignoring failures causes more harm.

questions.stem: What does "change collision" mean?
options: A change approved by two different managers
A change created from a standard template
A change and an incident with the same number
Two changes on one CI at once
questions.explanation: Collisions are scheduling conflicts on shared CIs, which conflict detection flags. Numbering, dual approvals, and templates aren't collisions.

questions.stem: Which statement about standard changes is true?
options: They must always be authorized by a full CAB
They come from approved templates
They're only used during a major incident
They can't be linked to any CIs
questions.explanation: Users choose from the standard change catalog of pre-approved templates. They don't need CAB each time, aren't limited to major incidents, and can reference CIs.

questions.stem: What does a service request typically ask for?
options: An investigation into the root cause of incidents
Something standard, like access, software, or equipment
A fix for an unplanned outage affecting many users
An emergency change to production systems
questions.explanation: Requests are for standard, pre-defined items. Outages are incidents, root causes are problems, and production changes go through change management.

questions.stem: Which record represents one item a user ordered within a request?
options: A request (REQ)
A requested item (RITM)
A catalog task (SCTASK)
An incident (INC)
questions.explanation: Each ordered item is a RITM within the parent REQ, and SCTASKs carry fulfillment work. Incidents are a separate process.

questions.stem: Who usually does the hands-on work to fulfill a requested item?
options: The problem manager for the service
The CAB, during its weekly meeting
The requester, by updating the RITM
The fulfillment groups, via tasks
questions.explanation: Catalog tasks route work to fulfillment teams. Requesters, CAB, and problem managers don't fulfill catalog items.

questions.stem: What usually defines the steps to fulfill a catalog item?
options: The requester's notification settings
The CMDB Health score for the item
The item's picture and description
A flow attached to the item
questions.explanation: Flows (or legacy workflows) handle approvals, tasks, and automation. Pictures, notifications, and health scores don't drive fulfillment.

questions.stem: A laptop request needs the requester's manager to approve it. How is this usually done?
options: An approval step in the item's fulfillment flow
A note asking the manager to call the service desk
A UI policy that hides the item from managers
A change request raised for each laptop order
questions.explanation: Flows request approvals from the right person based on the requester. Notes, UI policies, or change requests aren't approval mechanisms for catalog items.

questions.stem: A new hire needs several items ordered together. What catalog feature fits?
options: An order guide
A variable set
A record producer
A UI action
questions.explanation: Order guides collect information once and order related items together. Record producers create other records, variable sets reuse questions, and UI actions add buttons.

questions.stem: Users should report outages from the catalog, creating incidents rather than requests. What should be built?
options: A catalog item with an approval
A record producer for incidents
An order guide with incident items
A variable set on the incident form
questions.explanation: Record producers create records on other tables, like incident, from a catalog-style form. Catalog items create RITMs, and the other features don't create incidents.

questions.stem: What are catalog variables?
options: Reports showing the most-ordered catalog items
Questions that collect information on an item
System properties that control the catalog's look
Approval rules for items above a certain price
questions.explanation: Variables are the questions on catalog forms whose answers drive fulfillment. Properties, approvals, and reports are separate.

questions.stem: How can a catalog item be shown only to employees in Finance?
options: By hiding it with a client script
By deleting it for everyone else
With user criteria on the item
By renaming the item "Finance only"
questions.explanation: User criteria control who can see and order items. Names, client scripts, or deletions don't reliably restrict access.

questions.stem: What helps users see where their request is in the fulfillment process?
options: The system log entries for the request
Stages shown on the request in the portal
The change schedule for that week
The CMDB record for the requester's laptop
questions.explanation: Stage displays show progress, such as waiting for approval or fulfillment. Logs, CMDB records, and change schedules don't show request progress to users.

questions.stem: Why should catalog items show an expected delivery time?
options: To set user expectations
To pause SLAs automatically
To assign the requester
To approve the request
questions.explanation: Delivery times help users plan and reduce follow-up calls. They don't pause SLAs, approve, or assign anything.

questions.stem: Where do most users browse the catalog and submit requests?
options: A portal like Employee Center
The CI Class Manager in the CMDB
The CAB Workbench for change managers
The backend list of sc_req_item records
questions.explanation: Portals give users a friendly catalog experience. Backend lists, Class Manager, and CAB Workbench are for fulfillers and admins.

questions.stem: Several catalog items ask the same delivery questions. What helps reuse them?
options: A variable set
A record producer
An order guide
A business rule
questions.explanation: Variable sets let you define questions once and add them to many items. Order guides bundle items, record producers create records, and business rules run server logic.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a request and an incident from the user's point of view?
options: A request asks for something; an incident reports something broken
There's no difference; users pick either one at random
A request is always free; an incident always costs money to fix
A request is anonymous; an incident always shows the user's name
questions.explanation: Users request standard things and report disruptions as incidents. Cost, anonymity, and randomness don't define them.

questions.stem: A requested item is rejected by the approver. What typically happens?
options: The item doesn't proceed to fulfillment
The item becomes an incident automatically
The approver must fulfill it personally
The item is fulfilled anyway after a delay
questions.explanation: Rejection stops fulfillment, and the requester is notified. It isn't fulfilled anyway, converted, or handed to the approver.

questions.stem: What makes a good catalog item?
options: A long technical description written for the fulfiller
No description, so users call the desk for details
Clear text, needed questions, defined fulfillment
As many questions as possible, so nothing is ever missed
questions.explanation: Good items are clear, concise, and backed by a defined fulfillment process. Too many questions, jargon, or missing descriptions drive confusion and calls.

questions.stem: How can request fulfillment be sped up for common items, like software installs?
options: Ask users to install the software themselves
Automate fulfillment with flows and integrations
Remove all approvals from every item
Close requests before fulfillment completes
questions.explanation: Automation — such as software deployment integrations — cuts manual effort. Removing all approvals, shifting work to users, or closing early isn't the answer.

questions.stem: What does request management's "request" (REQ) record mainly represent?
options: The knowledge article for the item
The user's overall order
The approval decision made by a manager
A single task done by a fulfillment team
questions.explanation: The REQ is like a shopping cart order; RITMs are items and SCTASKs are tasks. Approvals and knowledge are separate.

questions.stem: What's a benefit of moving common incidents, like password resets, to self-service?
options: Fewer calls and faster help for users
Less need for a knowledge base
Higher SLA breach rates
More incidents logged for reporting
questions.explanation: Self-service resolves routine needs instantly, reducing desk workload. It shouldn't increase incidents or breaches, and knowledge remains important.

questions.stem: Which statement about catalog item approvals is true?
options: Every catalog item must have exactly three approvals
Approvals are required only for free items
Approvals can only be given by the requester
They can be conditional, based on cost or item type
questions.explanation: Approvals can depend on conditions, such as requiring finance approval above a cost threshold. Fixed counts, self-approval, or free-only approvals aren't how it works.

questions.stem: How does Virtual Agent support request management?
options: It replaces the catalog for all items
It fulfills hardware requests physically
It lets users make common requests in a chat
It approves every request automatically
questions.explanation: Virtual Agent conversations can submit requests and answer questions. It doesn't auto-approve, replace the catalog, or deliver hardware.

questions.stem: What's the main purpose of request management metrics, such as average fulfillment time?
options: Setting incident priorities
Choosing which items to remove from CMDB
Ranking users by how often they order
Finding bottlenecks to improve delivery
questions.explanation: Fulfillment metrics show where requests stall — approvals, specific teams — so they can be improved. They aren't for ranking users, CMDB, or incidents.

questions.stem: What do SLA definitions specify?
options: Which knowledge articles to attach
Which agents are allowed to work a task
When the timer starts, pauses, and stops
Which CIs a task is permitted to affect
questions.explanation: SLA definitions set conditions and durations for measuring time on tasks. Assignment rights, CI scope, and knowledge are separate.

questions.stem: An SLA should count only business hours, 8 to 5 on weekdays. What should be set?
options: A higher priority on every task
A new SLA for each day of the week
A schedule on the SLA definition
A pause condition for every evening
questions.explanation: Schedules make the SLA count only working hours. Priority changes, manual pauses, or separate daily SLAs are workarounds.

questions.stem: What's the difference between an SLA and an OLA?
options: An OLA covers incidents; an SLA covers requests only
There's no difference; they're the same agreement
An SLA is internal; an OLA is with external vendors only
An SLA is with the customer; an OLA is between internal teams
questions.explanation: SLAs commit to customers, OLAs to internal teams supporting them, and underpinning contracts to external suppliers.

questions.stem: What is an underpinning contract?
options: An agreement with an external supplier
An agreement between two internal teams
An agreement with the end customer
A contract to buy the ServiceNow license
questions.explanation: Underpinning contracts cover supplier commitments supporting your SLAs. Internal agreements are OLAs, customer agreements are SLAs.

questions.stem: Which table stores the SLA records attached to individual tasks?
options: task_sla
contract_sla
sys_user_group
cmdb_ci_service
questions.explanation: task_sla holds the SLA instances running on tasks. contract_sla holds SLA definitions, and the other tables store groups and services.

questions.stem: What happens when an SLA's stop condition is met?
options: It completes and records any breach
The task is reassigned to another group
The task is closed automatically
The SLA restarts from zero immediately
questions.explanation: Meeting the stop condition ends the timer and records the outcome. It doesn't restart, close, or reassign the task.

questions.stem: An SLA was attached late, but should measure from when the incident was created. What setting helps?
options: A different schedule
A new pause condition
Retroactive start
A shorter target duration
questions.explanation: Retroactive start lets the SLA begin from an earlier time, such as the record's creation. Changing duration, pause, or schedule doesn't backdate the start.

questions.stem: How can teams be warned before an SLA breaches?
options: Notifications at 50% and 75%
A change to the task's priority
A pause condition that stops the timer
A report run after the SLA has breached
questions.explanation: SLA flows or workflows can notify at thresholds so teams act in time. Post-breach reports, pauses, or priority changes don't warn proactively.

questions.stem: What does an SLA's reset condition do?
options: Marks the SLA as breached immediately
Pauses the SLA until the caller replies
Deletes the task the SLA is attached to
Cancels it and starts a new one
questions.explanation: Reset conditions — for example, when priority changes — cancel the running SLA so the appropriate one starts. They don't pause, breach, or delete.

questions.stem: Why pause an incident SLA when it's waiting on the caller?
options: So the caller can see the agent's notes
So the incident's priority is lowered
So teams aren't timed while they wait
So the incident is closed without a resolution
questions.explanation: Pausing keeps measurement fair. It doesn't close, expose notes, or reprioritize.

questions.stem: What's the difference between business elapsed time and actual elapsed time on an SLA?
options: Business time includes weekends; actual excludes them
Business time counts only scheduled hours; actual counts all
There's no difference between the two values
Actual time is set by the agent; business time by the system
questions.explanation: Business elapsed time follows the SLA's schedule; actual elapsed time is wall-clock. The other descriptions are wrong.

questions.stem: Which timezone does an SLA usually use when calculating time?
options: The timezone of the server in the datacenter
The timezone source set on the definition
The timezone of the CAB chairperson
The timezone of the last agent to view it
questions.explanation: SLA definitions specify a timezone source, such as the caller's or the schedule's. Server, viewer, or CAB timezones aren't used.

questions.stem: Different priorities need different targets — 4 hours for P1, 8 for P2. How is this usually set up?
options: Separate SLA definitions with priority conditions
A UI policy that changes the timer on screen
One SLA whose target changes by hand each time
A knowledge article listing the targets
questions.explanation: Separate definitions with start conditions per priority apply the right target automatically. Manual edits, UI policies, or articles don't enforce targets.

questions.stem: What does an SLA "breach" mean?
options: The SLA was attached late
The task was completed early
The target time passed
The SLA was paused at least once
questions.explanation: A breach means the commitment wasn't met. Early completion, pauses, and late attachment aren't breaches.

questions.stem: What's a good way to monitor SLA performance across teams?
options: Checking the CMDB for SLA fields on CIs
Reports or dashboards on SLA achievement by group
Asking team leads to estimate their performance
Reading each task's SLA record one by one
questions.explanation: Aggregated reporting shows trends and problem areas. Manual review, estimates, or CMDB fields don't measure SLA performance.

questions.stem: Which metric measures how long incidents take to resolve on average?
options: First contact resolution
Mean time to resolve
Change success rate
Catalog item popularity
questions.explanation: MTTR tracks resolution speed. Change success, FCR, and catalog popularity measure other things.

questions.stem: Why use Performance Analytics for ITSM KPIs?
options: It tracks scores over time
It approves changes based on past scores
It replaces the incident and change tables
It closes incidents that exceed targets
questions.explanation: PA collects historical scores for trend analysis. It doesn't replace tables, approve changes, or close incidents.

questions.stem: What does an ITSM PA content pack provide?
options: Additional catalog items for users
A replacement for SLA definitions
A new set of incident states for agents
Prebuilt ITSM indicators
questions.explanation: Content packs supply ready-made ITSM indicators and dashboards. They don't change states, add catalog items, or replace SLAs.

questions.stem: Which metric shows how much open work a team has right now?
options: Number of standard change templates
Number of CAB meetings this year
Backlog of open incidents and tasks
Number of knowledge articles retired
questions.explanation: Backlog shows current workload. Retired articles, templates, and meeting counts don't.

questions.stem: A manager wants to see incidents by priority and assignment group in one view. Which report type fits?
options: A pivot or grouped bar chart
A list with no grouping or filters
A single score showing total incidents
A calendar of change requests
questions.explanation: Pivots or grouped charts show two dimensions. Single scores, flat lists, and change calendars don't.

questions.stem: Why should KPIs be tied to targets?
options: To reduce the number of reports
To show if targets are met
To lock the data from further changes
To make dashboards more colorful
questions.explanation: Targets turn measurements into goals and make gaps visible. Color, data locking, and report counts aren't the reason.

questions.stem: What does a rising reopen rate for incidents suggest?
options: More users are using self-service
Agents are resolving incidents faster
Fixes may not be solving the issue
Changes are being approved more quickly
questions.explanation: Reopens often mean incidents were closed prematurely or not truly fixed. The other interpretations don't follow.

questions.stem: Which audience most needs a dashboard of SLA breaches and backlog by team?
options: The CMDB discovery service account
Service desk and team managers
End users browsing the catalog
External vendors' sales teams
questions.explanation: Managers act on breaches and backlog. End users, vendor sales teams, and service accounts don't.

questions.stem: What's the value of breaking down metrics by service?
options: It shows troubled services
It deletes services with few incidents
It changes each service's CMDB class
It hides incidents with no service
questions.explanation: Service breakdowns point improvement efforts at troubled services. They don't change classes, hide records, or delete services.

questions.stem: Which metric best reflects change management quality?
options: Average length of change descriptions
Number of approvers per change
Percentage of changes causing incidents
Number of changes raised per day
questions.explanation: Changes that cause incidents indicate quality problems. Volume, description length, and approver counts don't measure quality.

questions.stem: Why schedule ITSM reports to stakeholders?
options: They get regular updates without logging in
It makes the data in the reports more accurate
Scheduled reports can't be viewed in the platform
Scheduled reports approve changes automatically
questions.explanation: Scheduled delivery keeps stakeholders informed. It doesn't restrict viewing, change accuracy, or approve anything.

questions.stem: What does customer satisfaction survey data add to ITSM reporting?
options: The risk score of upcoming changes
The CMDB health of affected CIs
The user's view of service quality
The technical root cause of incidents
questions.explanation: Surveys capture how users experience service, complementing operational metrics. Root causes, change risk, and CMDB health come from elsewhere.

questions.stem: Where can agents see their own workload and performance in recent releases?
options: The update set list for the instance
The system log for their user account
The CI Class Manager in the CMDB
The workspace dashboards
questions.explanation: Workspace dashboards and lists give agents their queues and metrics. Logs, Class Manager, and update sets aren't for this.

questions.stem: What's a risk of measuring agents only on the number of incidents closed?
options: It reduces the number of reopened incidents
It makes agents spend more time on each incident
It can encourage closing incidents without real fixes
It improves first contact resolution automatically
questions.explanation: Volume-only metrics reward premature closure and gaming. Balanced metrics — quality, reopen rate, satisfaction — reduce that risk.

questions.stem: Which metric shows how quickly the service desk answers new incidents?
options: Time to respond
Knowledge article views
Mean time between failures
Change success rate
questions.explanation: Time to respond measures how quickly work starts. MTBF measures reliability, change success measures change quality, and article views measure knowledge use.

questions.stem: An approved normal change is ready but needs a date. Which state does it move to once it's planned?
options: Scheduled
Implement
Review
Assess
questions.explanation: After authorization, a change is scheduled for implementation. Assess comes earlier, and Implement and Review follow scheduling.
